summary.plain: A ring-shaped particle accelerator at Brookhaven National Laboratory, running since 1960. It once held the world speed record for protons and its experiments won three Nobel Prizes; today it accelerates particles before feeding them into other machines, including the RHIC collider.

summary.plain: Jefferson Lab's main particle accelerator, which fires a continuous beam of electrons at nuclear targets in three (now four) experimental halls. It began at 4 GeV, was raised to 6 GeV in 2000, and was upgraded again to 12 GeV in 2018.

summary.plain: A rapid-cycling ring 474 metres around that takes protons to 8 billion electronvolts. It feeds the Booster neutrino beam and the rest of the Fermilab chain.

summary.plain: The first machine in the Fermilab chain: it turns hydrogen ions into a 400-million-electronvolt beam and passes them to the next accelerator.

start.display: in operation by 2005; commissioning date not sourced

summary.plain: A 3.3-kilometre ring that accelerates protons to 120 billion electronvolts. Its beam makes the NuMI neutrinos today and will make the LBNF beam for DUNE.

summary.plain: A fixed-energy storage ring sitting in the same tunnel as the Main Injector. It stacks protons while the Main Injector accelerates, so the neutrino beam can be made faster.
The proton-antiproton collider that was the most powerful in the world until the LHC. It ran at Fermilab until 2011 and was where the top quark was found.

A major upgrade of the Large Hadron Collider now being installed. By replacing about 1.2 kilometres of the ring with new magnets and equipment it will squeeze the beams harder so that many more collisions happen each second, giving the experiments roughly ten times more data.

The world's first machine to collide two beams of protons head-on, built at CERN and running from 1971 to 1984. It convinced physicists that colliding hadrons could work, and it held the record for collision rate among hadron colliders until 2004.
The first machine in the J-PARC chain: a 300-metre linear accelerator that gives hydrogen ions their initial energy before they are passed to the ring accelerators.

operation at 760 kW after the 2023 beamline upgrade

summary.plain: The largest J-PARC accelerator: a 1.6-kilometre ring that accelerates protons to 30 billion electronvolts and fires them at the target that makes the neutrino beam.
A fast-cycling ring that takes protons from the linac up to 3 billion electronvolts 25 times a second, feeding both a neutron source and the main ring.

KEK's first big accelerator, a proton ring finished in 1976. From 1999 it produced the neutrino beam for K2K, the first experiment to send neutrinos hundreds of kilometres to a distant detector. Experiments ended in 2005.

intervals.label: shut down for the SuperKEKB upgrade

summary.plain: A three-kilometre-long machine at the KEK laboratory in Japan that smashed electrons into positrons at different energies from 1998 to 2010. It made huge numbers of B mesons for the Belle experiment and set a world record for collision rate.

A long particle accelerator at Los Alamos National Laboratory that fires protons at high energy. Originally built to study the strong nuclear force, it later produced the neutrino beam for the LSND experiment and today serves nuclear-security and materials research.

The largest electron-positron collider ever built: a 27-kilometre ring under the Swiss-French border that ran from 1989 to 2000 and produced about 17 million Z particles. Its tunnel was then reused for the Large Hadron Collider.

The world's largest and most powerful particle accelerator: a 27-kilometre ring of superconducting magnets under the Swiss-French border that steers two beams of protons in opposite directions and smashes them together inside four large experiments, including ATLAS.

The straight accelerator that started every proton used in CERN's experiments for forty years. It took protons up to 50 million electronvolts and passed them to the Proton Synchrotron Booster, and it was switched off for the last time in November 2018.

An 86-metre straight accelerator, 12 metres underground, that is the first step for every proton used at CERN. It accelerates hydrogen ions to 160 million electronvolts and has been the source of the beams that end up in the Large Hadron Collider since 2020.
A particle collider at SLAC that smashed together electrons and positrons at slightly different energies to produce large numbers of B mesons, studied by the BaBar detector from 1999 to 2008.

CERN's oldest working accelerator, a 628-metre ring that first accelerated protons in 1959. For a short time it was the most powerful accelerator in the world, and it still feeds every beam that ends up in the Large Hadron Collider.

summary.plain: Four small accelerator rings stacked on top of each other that take particles from the linear accelerator and give them their first big push before the Proton Synchrotron. Adding the Booster in 1972 let CERN put more than a hundred times as many protons into the next machine.

summary.plain: A giant underground ring at Brookhaven National Laboratory that collided beams of gold atomic nuclei and of protons with aligned spins at nearly the speed of light, recreating conditions from just after the Big Bang. It ran from 2000 to 2026 and is now being rebuilt into a new machine, the Electron-Ion Collider.

SLAC's two-mile-long linear accelerator, which fires electrons (and, in its early years, positrons) down a straight underground tunnel. It has fed three generations of SLAC's experiments: the original fixed-target program, the SLC and PEP-II colliders, and today the LCLS X-ray laser.

A particle collider at SLAC that smashed together beams of electrons and positrons tuned to the mass of the Z boson, letting physicists study that particle's properties with the SLD detector from 1989 to 1998.

summary.plain: A powerful particle accelerator at Oak Ridge National Laboratory that fires pulses of protons into a liquid-mercury target to produce neutrons for research. The same process also produces a very pure, well-timed source of neutrinos used by experiments such as COHERENT.

A seven-kilometre ring at CERN that has been the laboratory's workhorse since 1976. It accelerates protons to 450 billion electronvolts and hands them to the Large Hadron Collider, and in the 1980s it was rebuilt to collide protons with antiprotons, which is how the W and Z particles were discovered.

summary.plain: The rebuilt version of the KEKB collider in Japan. It squeezes its electron and positron beams down to nanometre thinness so they collide far more often than before, and since 2020 it has held the world record for collision rate.

beamline:kek-neutrino.target: Aluminium rod, 66 cm long and 3 cm in diameter, inside the first of two focusing horns

The DESY-based collaboration that ran ALPS I and now runs ALPS II, searching for very light, weakly interacting particles with laser light.
The team of scientists, led from the University of Hawai'i, who built and flew the ANITA balloon-borne neutrino detector over Antarctica five times between 2003 and 2016.
The roughly 150 scientists and engineers, from institutes in about eight countries, who built and ran the ANTARES undersea neutrino telescope from 1996 until it was switched off in 2022.
The team of scientists, including the group at UW-Madison's IceCube centre, who built and continue to run the ARA radio-antenna stations near the South Pole.
The team of scientists, based at UC Irvine and partner institutions, who built and ran the now-decommissioned ARIANNA pilot neutrino experiment on the Ross Ice Shelf.

The international team that built and runs the ATLAS experiment. It counts its birthday as 1 October 1992, the day it handed CERN its Letter of Intent, and today it has more than 5500 members from over 170 institutions in about 40 countries.

More than 500 scientists, engineers and graduate students from about 10 countries who built and ran the BaBar particle detector at SLAC from 1999 to 2008 to study why matter and antimatter behave differently.
The Russian-led international team of scientists building and running the Baikal-GVD neutrino telescope in Lake Baikal.
The international team of physicists who built and ran the Belle detector at the KEK laboratory in Japan and analysed its data.
The worldwide team running the Belle II experiment in Japan: more than 1100 scientists and engineers from 122 institutions in 27 countries.
The international team of scientists, including founders Gianpaolo Bellini and Frank Calaprice, who built and ran the Borexino solar-neutrino experiment in Italy.
The international group of physicists who built and ran the CAST solar-axion search at CERN from 2003 to 2022.

About 600 physicists and engineers from roughly 60 institutions in 15 countries who built and ran the CDF particle detector at Fermilab from the 1980s until the Tevatron collider shut down in 2011, and who still analyze the data it recorded.
The group of physicists who built and ran the CDMS II dark matter detector at the Soudan mine in Minnesota from the mid-2000s to 2009.
The international team that built and runs the CMS experiment: several thousand physicists, engineers and students from hundreds of universities and laboratories in more than sixty countries.
The international team of physicists who built and run the COHERENT experiment: 21 institutions in 4 countries, formed in 2013 to measure how neutrinos scatter off whole atomic nuclei.
The more than 290 researchers, from 48 institutes, building the COMET experiment at J-PARC in Japan.
The physicists who built and run the CONUS and CONUS+ reactor-neutrino experiments, led from the Max Planck Institute for Nuclear Physics in Germany.
The international team of physicists, based partly at the Max Planck Institute in Munich, who run the CRESST dark matter search under the Gran Sasso mountain in Italy.
The international organisation of countries and institutes building and running CTAO, the next-generation gamma-ray observatory.
The physicists who built and run the CUORE tellurium-crystal experiment deep under the Gran Sasso mountain in Italy.
The team preparing CUPID, the planned successor to CUORE, which will search for a rare radioactive process using lithium-molybdate crystals in Italy.

About 540 physicists and engineers from roughly 90 institutions in 18 countries who built and ran the D0 particle detector at Fermilab from 1992 until the Tevatron collider shut down in 2011, and who still analyze the data it recorded.

The team of physicists who ran the DAMIC silicon-CCD dark matter search, first at Fermilab and then at SNOLAB in Canada, from 2008 until around 2025, when the SNOLAB detector was repurposed as a test stand.
The team of physicists running the DAMIC-M dark matter search under a mountain in the French Alps.
The international team of scientists that built and ran the DarkSide-50 dark matter detector and is now building its much larger successor, DarkSide-20k, both deep under an Italian mountain.
The international team of scientists from China and several other countries who built and ran the Daya Bay reactor-neutrino experiment.
The international team that built and runs the DEAP-3600 dark matter detector at SNOLAB in Canada, made up of scientists from institutions in about ten countries.
The international team of about 550 physicists from 56 institutes who built and ran the DELPHI detector at CERN's LEP collider.
The Stanford/SLAC-based team developing the DMRadio family of lumped-element axion dark-matter searches.
The physicists who ran the DONUT experiment at Fermilab in 1997 and, in 2001, published the first direct observation of tau-neutrino interactions.
The international team of scientists who built and ran the Double Chooz reactor-neutrino experiment in France.
The international team of more than 1500 scientists and engineers, from 228 institutions in 38 countries, that designs, builds and will run the DUNE experiment.
The team of physicists who ran the E949 rare-kaon-decay experiment at Brookhaven, continuing the earlier E787 collaboration.
The French-led team of physicists running the EDELWEISS germanium dark matter search under a mountain in the French Alps.
The team of physicists who built and ran the EXO-200 xenon neutrino experiment in a New Mexico salt mine from 2011 to 2018.
The scientists who proposed, built and run the FASER experiment at CERN.
The international team, led by the Max Planck Institute for Nuclear Physics in Heidelberg, that ran the GALLEX and GNO gallium solar-neutrino experiments in Italy.
Around 120 scientists from 16 institutes in six European countries who built and ran the GERDA neutrino experiment under the Gran Sasso mountain in Italy.
The international team of scientists proposing and prototyping the GRAND giant radio array for detecting cosmic rays and neutrinos.
The roughly 200 scientists, engineers and students from more than a dozen countries who built and run the H.E.S.S. gamma-ray telescopes in Namibia.
The physicists and engineers who built and ran the H1 particle detector at DESY, in Germany, from 1992 until the HERA collider shut down in 2007.
The scientists who built and run the HAWC gamma-ray observatory on a Mexican volcano.
The collaboration of Yale, UC Berkeley, Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, and University of Colorado Boulder scientists running the HAYSTAC axion search.
The small team led by Ray Davis (experiment) and John Bahcall (theory) that ran the Homestake chlorine experiment for over two decades.
The international team building Hyper-Kamiokande: about 680 researchers who have taken part from over 140 institutes in 23 countries.
The international collaboration developing the IAXO axion helioscope and its BabyIAXO prototype at DESY, formally established in 2017.
The international team, originally led by Nobel laureate Carlo Rubbia, that built the ICARUS liquid-argon detector, ran it in Italy, rebuilt it at CERN, and now runs it at Fermilab.
The international team that runs the IceCube telescope at the South Pole: about 450 scientists at 58 universities and laboratories in 14 countries. It grew out of the earlier AMANDA team in 1999.
The international team of more than 700 scientists from 75 institutions in 17 countries and regions who built and run the JUNO neutrino experiment.
The Japan-Korea-US team that built and ran K2K, the world's first long-baseline neutrino oscillation experiment, from 1999 to 2004.
The team of scientists, based at Tohoku University's Research Center for Neutrino Science, who built and run the KamLAND experiment in Japan.
The physicists who run the KamLAND-Zen search for a rare radioactive process in xenon, using the KamLAND detector in Japan.
The physicists from Karlsruhe, Oxford, London, Erlangen and Bonn who built and ran the KARMEN neutrino detector at the ISIS accelerator in England from 1990 to 2001.
More than 150 scientists, engineers and students from 12 institutions in four countries who run the KATRIN neutrino-mass experiment in Germany.

The international team of about 250 scientists from 39 institutions in six countries that built and runs the LZ dark matter detector in South Dakota.
The scientists who built and run the MAGIC gamma-ray telescopes on La Palma.
The team of scientists who built and ran the Majorana Demonstrator germanium neutrino experiment in South Dakota; many went on to join the follow-on LEGEND experiment.

The team, co-led by Janet Conrad and Bill Louis, that built and ran the MiniBooNE detector at Fermilab from 2002 to 2019 to test a puzzling earlier neutrino result.

The scientists who built and run the MoEDAL experiment, searching for magnetic monopoles at CERN's LHC.

Over 150 scientists from 31 institutions in 8 countries designing the next-generation nEXO xenon neutrino experiment, planned for Canada's SNOLAB.
About 100 scientists from more than 20 institutions in six countries who built and run the NEXT xenon-gas neutrino experiment in Spain.
The 203 scientists and engineers, from 53 institutions in nine countries, who built and run the NOvA neutrino experiment.
The physicists building and commissioning the NUCLEUS experiment, a very sensitive, very small reactor-neutrino detector at a French nuclear plant.
The international team of about 200 physicists from 34 institutes who built and ran the OPAL detector at CERN's LEP collider.
The international team of physicists, based at CERN and Gran Sasso, who built and ran the OPERA tau-neutrino detector from 2008 to 2012.
The international team of scientists, based partly at TRIUMF and partner universities, planning and building the P-ONE neutrino telescope for the deep Pacific Ocean.
The team of scientists, led from Shanghai Jiao Tong University, that built and runs the PandaX-4T dark matter detector in China.

The roughly 400 scientists and engineers from 17 countries who built and run the Pierre Auger Observatory, the world's largest cosmic-ray detector.
The scientists and engineers from institutions including MIT, the University of Washington, UC Santa Barbara, Yale and PNNL who are developing the Project 8 neutrino-mass experiment.
The team of South Korean and international scientists who built and run the RENO reactor-neutrino experiment.
The physicists building and commissioning the Ricochet reactor-neutrino experiment at a French research reactor.
The international team of scientists building and running the RNO-G radio neutrino detector on the Greenland ice sheet.
The Russian-American team, including physicists Vladimir Gavrin, Georgiy Zatsepin and Thomas Bowles, who built and run the SAGE gallium solar-neutrino experiment.

The scientists who built and run the SND@LHC experiment at CERN.

The international team of about 240 physicists from roughly 60 institutions in 11 countries who run the Super-Kamiokande detector.
The international team of scientists running the SuperCDMS dark matter search, first at the Soudan mine in Minnesota and now at SNOLAB in Canada.

The international team of physicists who built and ran the UA2 detector at CERN, co-discovering the W and Z bosons with the UA1 Collaboration.
The scientists who built and run the VERITAS gamma-ray telescope array in Arizona.
The international team of scientists that has built and run a series of ever-larger liquid xenon dark matter detectors at Gran Sasso in Italy: XENON10, XENON100, XENON1T and now XENONnT.
About 450 physicists who built and ran the ZEUS particle detector at DESY, in Germany, from 1992 until the HERA collider shut down in 2007.

detector:abracadabra.name: ABRACADABRA-10 cm apparatus

summary.plain: ABRACADABRA-10 cm was a small prototype detector at MIT that looked for a tiny magnetic signal that dark-matter axions would produce inside a toroidal magnet. It finished its axion search around 2021.

detector:abracadabra.technology: Lumped-element (broadband/resonant) toroidal magnetometer: a toroidal magnet with a SQUID-based pickup at its center senses the small oscillating magnetic field an axion dark-matter background would induce, rather than using a resonant microwave cavity.

detector:admx.name: ADMX detector

summary.plain: The ADMX detector uses a powerful magnet and a supercooled tunable metal cavity to try to convert dark-matter axions into faint microwave signals, which are then amplified and measured.

detector:admx.technology: Microwave-cavity haloscope: a tunable, cylindrical copper-plated resonant cavity inside a large superconducting solenoid magnet, read out through a dilution refrigerator and a near-quantum-limited (Josephson parametric / SQUID) amplifier chain.

detector:aleph.name: ALEPH detector

specs.calorimeters: Electromagnetic calorimeter to identify electrons and photons; hadron calorimeter to detect hadrons
specs.tracker: Silicon-microstrip vertex detector (two double-sided layers), 8-coordinate inner drift chamber with trigger, and a 4.4 m x 3.6 m time projection chamber

subsystems.description: 4.4 m long, 3.6 m in diameter, the central charged-particle tracker.
subsystems.name: Time projection chamber

subsystems.description: 6.3 m long, 5.3 m in diameter, providing a 1.5 T magnetic field.
subsystems.name: Superconducting solenoid

summary.plain: A cylindrical, general-purpose detector at LEP's Point 4, built around a giant gas chamber and a superconducting magnet to track and identify particles from electron-positron collisions.

detector:aleph.technology: General-purpose collider detector with a large-volume time projection chamber inside a superconducting solenoid
